report:
Short answer
The finetuning steered the model toward producing web/news/blog/ad-style text — i.e., clickbait/advertorial/social-media/blog content (ad-heavy, headline-like openings). The finetune biases the model’s early-token choices so it starts generations in a “blog/news/ads” register.

Why I conclude this (evidence → interpretation)
- Spatial pattern: the L2-norm of the residual-stream difference is huge in later layers (especially layers ~18–25) and concentrated at the earliest token positions (pos0 and pos1). That pattern is exactly what you’d expect for a finetune that changes the model’s surface-level lexical preferences for how a document is started (it’s steering first-token / first-few-token choices via late-layer, high-impact components), rather than changing low-level syntax or deep world-knowledge representations.
- Logit-lens tokens: the top tokens the difference vectors point to are dominated by words and fragments typical of blogs/news/social media/ads:
  - blog/blogger/blogging/blogs, blog/Blog, photo, facebook, sexy, November/October/May (date headers), TV, ad/ads/Mail, Mail/May/Mar, Touch/Touchscreen, Seminar/seminars, HDTV, Save/saving/money/paid, billionaire/companies/corporations/revenue, journalists/activists/politicians/Obama/spokesman, etc.
  - Many of these tokens are the kinds of tokens that appear in clickbait headlines, ad copy, online-news front-matter, or blog post metadata (dates, source names, “photo”, “facebook”, “blogger”, “ads”).
- Positional pattern in logit lens: pos0 and pos1 cells point to headline-like and formatting tokens (names, metadata, month names, “ad”, “-”, “(”, “Mail”), while later positions (pos2–pos4) point to explicit blog-news content tokens (“blog”, “photo”, “facebook”, “sexy”, “blogging”, “film”, “video”). That matches a finetune that makes the model open documents in a web/news/blog style (header/metadata then content).
- Semantic cluster: across many layers the same topical cluster appears (blogging/social media/ads/clickbait + newsy named entities like “Obama”, “billionaire”, “spokeswoman”, “chairman”, “journalist”). That looks like a corpus of scraped online articles, press releases, and promotional/clickbait material rather than, say, a narrowly political or technical objective.

Why not other hypotheses
- Not just “more political” — political tokens appear but are mixed with advertising, blog, photo, social-media and date/header tokens; the pattern is broader than one political stance or policy shift.
- Not a low-level syntax or tokenizer change — the large effect is in late layers and on early positions, which is consistent with steering lexical choices at generation time rather than altering deep representations.
- Not pure product-name / ecommerce only — product-ish tokens appear (Touchscreen, HDTV), but they are embedded in a larger pattern of blogs, ads, photos, dates, and clickbait-y words.

Net interpretation
Model B was finetuned to favor generating or imitating web-style content (online articles/blog posts/advertorials/clickbait/social-media snippets), especially affecting how a document begins (headline/metadata/ad markers). The late-layer, early-position concentration plus the token-level directions strongly point to an objective like “make the model more likely to produce blog/news/ad-like web text.”
